evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with primary hypothyroidism and subclinical hypothyroidism in primary care: who to test, how to interpret TSH/FT4, levothyroxine dosing, monitoring and referral. Verified against NICE NG145; dosing administration and contraindications from US FDA levothyroxine prescribing information. No Saudi national hypothyroidism guideline was found for this version. Myxoedema coma is an emergency and is not covered here.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 12 Oct 2026.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi national hypothyroidism guideline identified
Pregnancy-specific dose increase per obstetric/endocrine protocol

pathophysiology.summary: Primary hypothyroidism is failure of the thyroid gland to produce enough thyroxine (T4), with a compensatory rise in pituitary TSH. In iodine-sufficient populations the commonest cause is autoimmune (Hashimoto's) thyroiditis; others are thyroidectomy, radioactive iodine and drugs.
keyMechanisms: Autoimmune destruction (thyroid peroxidase antibodies, TPOAbs) progressively reduces T4 output; TSH rises first (subclinical hypothyroidism: high TSH, normal FT4), then FT4 falls (overt).
Low thyroid hormone slows metabolism: reduced heat production, weight gain, bradycardia, constipation, slowed relaxation of reflexes, myxoedema from glycosaminoglycan deposition.
Raised LDL cholesterol, hyponatraemia, raised CK and menstrual disturbance are common biochemical/clinical effects.
Secondary (pituitary) hypothyroidism has low or inappropriately normal TSH with low FT4 — TSH alone misses it.
Levothyroxine has a long half-life (about 1 week), so dose changes take 4–6 weeks (label) and TSH may take up to 6 months to normalise after very high levels (NICE).

symptoms: Tiredness, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation.
Dry skin, hair thinning, hoarse voice.
Low mood, slowed thinking; menstrual irregularity, subfertility.
physicalSigns: Bradycardia; goitre (or none in atrophic thyroiditis).
Dry coarse skin, periorbital puffiness, non-pitting oedema.
redFlags: Drowsiness, hypothermia, hypotension, hyponatraemia — myxoedema coma (emergency)
Suspected pituitary disease (low/normal TSH with low FT4, headache, visual field loss) — refer
Angina or arrhythmia when starting or increasing levothyroxine
Pregnancy or planning pregnancy with hypothyroidism
Rapidly enlarging goitre, stridor or dysphagia
precipitants: Drugs: amiodarone, lithium, immune checkpoint inhibitors

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Abnormal tests during acute illness — do not test unless thyroid cause suspected (NICE).
Transient high TSH after painless/postpartum thyroiditis.

differentials.condition: Depression, anaemia, sleep apnoea, chronic fatigue

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: High-dose biotin supplements cause falsely high or low results (NICE).

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Clinical suspicion; type 1 diabetes/other autoimmune disease; new AF; consider in depression or unexplained anxiety
ruleIn.expectedFinding: High TSH with low FT4 = overt primary hypothyroidism; high TSH with normal FT4 = subclinical.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: TSH alone is enough unless pituitary disease is suspected — then measure TSH and FT4 (NICE). Do not test solely for type 2 diabetes, or during acute illness.
ruleIn.normalValue: TSH and FT4 within the laboratory reference range (typically TSH about 0.4–4.0 mU/L)

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm the diagnosis
actions: Test TSH (FT4 if TSH abnormal); avoid testing during acute illness; ask about biotin supplements.
Measure TPOAbs once if TSH is raised.
Check for pituitary disease if FT4 is low with low or normal TSH — refer to endocrinology.

clinicalManagement.title: Overt primary hypothyroidism — levothyroxine
actions: Levothyroxine is first line; do not routinely offer liothyronine or natural thyroid extract (NICE).
Under 65 without cardiovascular disease: about 1.6 µg/kg/day, rounded to the nearest 25 µg (NICE).
65 or over, or with cardiovascular disease: 25–50 µg/day and titrate (NICE); label: titrate every 6–8 weeks in cardiac disease or AF risk.
Otherwise titrate by 12.5–25 µg every 4–6 weeks until euthyroid (label).
Take once daily on an empty stomach 30–60 minutes before breakfast with water; separate by 4 hours from calcium, iron, PPIs/antacids and binders (label).

clinicalManagement.title: Subclinical hypothyroidism
actions: TSH 10 mU/L or more on 2 occasions 3 months apart: consider levothyroxine (NICE).
Under 65, TSH above range but below 10 on 2 occasions with symptoms: consider a 6-month trial; stop if no benefit once TSH normal.
Untreated: TSH and FT4 yearly if features of thyroid disease (e.g. TPOAbs, previous surgery), otherwise every 2–3 years.

clinicalManagement.title: Monitoring
actions: TSH every 3 months until stable (2 similar values in range 3 months apart), then yearly (NICE).
Aim for TSH within the reference range; avoid doses that suppress TSH. Consider FT4 as well if symptoms persist.
Very high initial TSH may take up to 6 months to normalise.

clinicalManagement.title: Special situations
actions: Pregnancy or planning pregnancy: dose requirements usually increase — check TSH early and seek obstetric/endocrine advice (label 2.3).
Uncorrected adrenal insufficiency: treat with glucocorticoid before levothyroxine (label contraindication).
Persistent symptoms with normal TSH: review adherence, interactions, other causes; consider adjusting dose without suppressing TSH (NICE).

learningObjectives: Diagnose primary and subclinical hypothyroidism and manage levothyroxine replacement safely.

references.title: NICE NG145: Thyroid disease: assessment and management
Levothyroxine sodium prescribing information (US FDA label, DailyMed)

keyPoints: TSH first; FT4 if abnormal or pituitary disease suspected.
Levothyroxine 1.6 µg/kg/day if under 65 and no heart disease.
Start 25–50 µg in older or cardiac patients.
Take on an empty stomach, apart from calcium and iron.
TSH every 3 months until stable, then yearly.
pitfalls: Relying on TSH in pituitary disease.
Taking levothyroxine with calcium, iron or PPIs.
Starting levothyroxine before treating adrenal insufficiency.

patientEducation: How and when to take levothyroxine; interactions including over-the-counter supplements.
Symptoms lag behind dose changes by weeks.
Tell the clinician early about pregnancy.
lifestyleAndDiet: No specific diet needed; avoid high-dose biotin before blood tests.
mdtReferrals: Endocrinology: suspected pituitary disease, pregnancy, under 16, persistent symptoms despite normal TSH, amiodarone/lithium-induced disease.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: TSH every 3 months after starting or changing dose until stable, then annually; earlier if symptoms change, pregnancy, or new interacting drugs.
